items.title: Why swapping two ingredients silently misplaces saved intent
items.body:
The key is right: the normalizer does nothing, because every `slug:index` key still exists, so saved intent attaches to the wrong items. Keys point at a **position**, not at an ingredient. If the cookbook swaps ingredients 0 and 1, `soup:0` and `soup:1` are both still valid keys, so `validKeys` keeps both entries. But each now points at the other ingredient: a checkmark or quantity the shopper set for the first ingredient now shows on the second. The worked change calls this the real limit of positional keys; stable per-ingredient ids would fix it.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Two overrides collide on one key": each entry keeps its own key; nothing collides.
- "Re-matched by ingredient name": nothing in the code compares names.
- "validKeys detects the swap": it only checks that the index exists, not what is at it.

excerpts.quote: if the cookbook *reordered* two ingredients instead of removing one, every index-based key would silently point at the wrong ingredient and nothing here would notice. That is the real limit of positional keys
.ingredients.map((_, i) => `${slug}:${i}`)

items.title: Start here: editable shopping quantities in a React recipe app
items.body:
Recipeweb is a React recipe app with a shopping list: pick recipes, tick off ingredients, and (after the change this course studies) edit the quantity text for any ingredient. The list is saved in the browser's `localStorage`. The course's central skill is **state ownership, storage validation and accessible controls**.

Suggested reading order (the chapters are numbered):

1. `astraupskill/README.md`: what you will be able to do, and how to run the project and its tests.
2. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: where the store, the screens and the tests live.
3. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: reference data versus user state, validation versus normalization, and the same job on a server.
4. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`, especially "Unpacking the densest line" and the three variations.
5. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`, then `05-PRACTICE.md` before `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`.

Most quizzes walk a specific stored document through `normalizeShoppingState` in `src/store/shoppingState.ts`. It is only 31 lines; read it until you can predict its output for any input.

excerpts.quote: The central skill is **React state ownership, storage validation and accessible controls**.
Run `npm install` and `npm run dev` from this project folder. Run `npm test` for its automated checks

readMore.why: Where each part of the shopping-list feature lives.
The worked change, line by line.

items.title: What an unguarded spread does with a string
items.body:
The key is right: `['s', 'o', 'u', 'p']`. Spread syntax (`[...x]`) works on anything **iterable**, and strings are iterable character by character. So spreading the string `'soup'` gives an array of its four letters. That is a quiet, wrong result: no error, just four bogus slugs. The `Array.isArray` guard turns a non-array into `[]` instead.

A precise note from the quiz's own explanation: the real code calls `.filter` on the value before spreading, and a string has no `filter` method, so without the guard the real line would actually throw. The guide's comparison is with a bare spread, which fails silently.

Why the others are wrong:
- "['soup']": spread does not wrap a value; it unpacks it.
- "An empty array": a string has elements to iterate, its characters.
- "A TypeError": spread accepts any iterable, strings included.

excerpts.quote: If the stored value is `{ recipeSlugs: 'soup' }` the answer is `[]`, not `['s','o','u','p']` - which is what `[...input.recipeSlugs]` alone would have produced, because strings are iterable.
const recipeSlugs = Array.isArray(input.recipeSlugs)

items.title: Why reset must delete the key instead of saving ''
items.body:
The key is right: an absent key falls back to the recipe amount, while `''` is itself a saved override. The concepts chapter defines two different states: no override means "use the recipe's quantity", and an empty-string override means "the shopper removed the text". Reset-to-recipe is the first state, so the solution removes the key from `quantities` and lets `??` fall back. Calling `setQuantity(key, '')` would instead store "cleared", and after a reload the shopper would see no quantity at all.

Why the others are wrong:
- "setQuantity cannot write empty strings": it only rejects values longer than 100 characters.
- "Only an optimisation to keep JSON small": the two states mean different things on screen.
- "Empty strings fail the length bound": `''.length` is 0, well within `<= 100`.

excerpts.quote: const { [key]: _removed, ...rest } = s.quantities;   // delete the key, do not blank it
An absent override uses the source recipe quantity; an explicit empty string means the shopper intentionally removed the quantity text.
if (value.length > 100) return;

items.title: What setQuantity does with a 150-character value
items.body:
The key is right: the handler returns early and state is untouched. `setQuantity` starts with `if (value.length > 100) return;`, the same 100-character bound the normalizer applies on load. A 150-character value fails it, so `setState` is never called: nothing is stored in memory, and nothing reaches storage. Valid values go through `normalizeShoppingState` too, so the write path and the load path share one set of rules.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Kept in memory, stripped on reload": it is never put in memory.
- "The normalizer throws": the normalizer never throws; it drops bad entries, and here it is not even reached.
- "Truncated to 100 characters": no code shortens the value; the concepts chapter says validation should not silently invent facts.

excerpts.quote: if (value.length > 100) return; setState((s) => normalizeShoppingState({ ...s, quantities: { ...s.quantities, [key]: value } }, RECIPES));
Validation rejects values the operation cannot accept.

items.title: Reference data, user overrides, and positional keys
items.body:
The cookbook is **reference data**: it ships with the app and the shopper cannot change it. The shopping list is **user state**. Instead of editing a recipe's ingredient array, the app stores a small override per ingredient. Read the display code to see exactly how it chooses between an override and the recipe's own text, and which operator it uses.

Each override and checkmark is stored under a key made of the recipe slug and the ingredient's position, like `soup:0` for soup's first ingredient. Read how the normalizer decides which saved keys to keep when it loads state, and where its list of valid keys comes from.

Two questions to answer for yourself as you read: is there a difference between a key that is *absent* and a key whose value is an *empty string*? And what happens to these positional keys when the cookbook changes, for example when an ingredient is removed, or when two are swapped? Work each case through the code before reading the worked change's discussion.

excerpts.quote: The cookbook is reference data; the shopping list is user state.
Quantity overrides are strings keyed by slug:index.
/** Use the same effective quantities for the screen and clipboard. */

readMore.why: Three variations to predict before running.

items.title: What the slug-is-string annotation is for
items.body:
The key is right: compilation breaks, because `filter` would return `unknown[]`, which cannot be assigned to `string[]`. The input array is `unknown[]`. A normal callback returning a boolean tells TypeScript nothing about the type of the items that pass, so `filter` still returns `unknown[]`. The annotation `(slug): slug is string` is a **type predicate**: it tells the compiler "every item this returns true for is a string", so the result becomes `string[]`, matching `ShoppingListState.recipeSlugs`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Runtime behaviour changes": annotations are erased when compiled; the same items are filtered either way.
- "The Set would compare differently": a Set compares values the same way whatever TypeScript thinks the type is.
- "Nothing; TypeScript infers it": the guide states that without it the assignment fails to compile.

excerpts.quote: The `: slug is string` return annotation is not decoration: without it, `filter` returns `unknown[]` and the assignment to `string[]` fails to compile.
recipeSlugs: string[];

items.title: Why stored JSON must be checked like any other input
items.body:
TypeScript checks your **source code** when you compile. It knows nothing about the bytes your program reads at runtime. Data from `localStorage` might be from an older version of the app, half-written, or edited by hand, so the honest type for it is `unknown`.

That is why the store passes everything it loads through a normalizer. The concepts chapter calls it a hand-written runtime schema and names the four steps every boundary needs: a **shape guard** (is this even an object or array?), a **type check** (is this field a string, a boolean?), a **domain check** (does this value refer to something that really exists?), and a **bound** (is it too long?).

The chapter then shows the same four steps as a Zod schema on an Express API, and points out two differences: what to do on failure, and who the untrusted party is. Keep those four steps in mind as a checklist; every quiz about the normalizer is one of them.

excerpts.quote: Every one of those boundaries needs the same four steps this normalizer performs - shape guard, type check, domain check, bound
The compiler checked your *source*; it did not check the bytes.
/** Treat browser storage as untrusted input, while retaining valid v1 data. */

readMore.why: The same job on a server, with a Zod example.

items.title: Why only a typeof-boolean check gets 'false' right
items.body:
The key is right: `'false'` is a truthy string, so a `Boolean(v)` check would mark the item checked. In JavaScript every non-empty string is truthy, including the text "false". So code written as `if (v)` or `Boolean(v)` would treat `'false'` as yes, the opposite of what was stored. The normalizer instead keeps a checked entry only if `typeof v === 'boolean'`; anything that is not a real boolean is dropped.

Why the others are wrong:
- "JSON stores booleans as the string 'false'": JSON has real `true` and `false` values; a string here means the data is wrong.
- "typeof keeps numbers": a number fails `typeof v === 'boolean'` and is dropped.
- "A truthiness check on 'false' would throw": truthiness checks never throw; they quietly give the wrong answer, which is worse.

excerpts.quote: validKeys.has(key) && typeof v === 'boolean'

and would also accept `'false'`, which is truthy too and would render the item as checked when the stored intent was the opposite. `typeof v === 'boolean'` is the only check that gets `'false'` right.

items.title: Why the display uses ?? instead of ||
items.body:
The key is right: an empty-string override is a real value, and `||` would bring back the recipe text. `ingredientsWithQuantities` uses `quantities[key] ?? ingredient.quantity`. The `??` operator only falls back when the left side is `null` or `undefined`, that is, when there is no override at all. `||` falls back on **any** falsy value, and the empty string is falsy. A shopper who deliberately cleared the text would see the recipe's quantity reappear.

Why the others are wrong:
- "They behave the same; overrides are never empty": an empty override is explicitly allowed and means "I cleared this".
- "?? is faster": speed is not the reason; meaning is.
- "|| cannot be used on strings": it can; it just gives the wrong answer here.

excerpts.quote: quantity: quantities[`${recipe.slug}:${index}`] ?? ingredient.quantity,
override ?? original respects an empty string, while override || original would silently restore text the user cleared.

items.title: What parseFloat does with '2 1/2 cups'
items.body:
The key is right: `2`. `parseFloat` reads a number from the start of a string and **stops at the first character it cannot use**, here the space. It never sees "1/2". So the fraction is silently lost, and doubling gives 4 cups when the recipe needs 5. The solutions chapter uses this as its first example of a broken implementation, and recommends a small parser that returns `null` for anything it does not understand, so the app can tell the shopper instead of guessing.

Why the others are wrong:
- "NaN": the string *starts* with a number, so parsing succeeds up to the space.
- "2.5": `parseFloat` does not understand mixed numbers or fractions.
- "A SyntaxError": `parseFloat` never throws on extra text; it ignores it.

excerpts.quote: `parseFloat('2 1/2 cups')` returns `2` - the fraction is silently dropped and the shopper buys 4 cups instead of 5
Quantity strings are intentionally not automatically parsed or scaled because values can contain fractions, ranges, package sizes and phrases such as "to taste".

items.title: What happens when localStorage refuses to save
items.body:
The key is right: the app catches the error, stays usable in memory, and sets a `storageError` flag. The provider saves state in an effect that runs whenever `state` changes. The write is inside `try`: on success it clears `storageError`; on failure (quota exceeded, private mode) the `catch` sets it to true. The in-memory state is untouched, so the list keeps working for the session; the flag lets the UI tell the shopper their progress is not being saved. The concepts chapter: storage failure is disclosed rather than hidden.

Why the others are wrong:
- "The exception propagates": the `catch` stops it.
- "Rolls back to the last saved snapshot": nothing reverts in-memory state.
- "Retries with backoff": the effect only runs again the next time state changes.

excerpts.quote: try { window.localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(state)); setStorageError(false); } catch { setStorageError(true); // Keep the current session usable; disclose persistence failure.
Storage failure is disclosed rather than hidden behind a claim that progress was saved.

items.title: What happens to keys for an ingredient that no longer exists
items.body:
The key is right: the slug survives, but both `soup:2` entries are dropped. On load, the normalizer builds `validKeys` from **today's** cookbook: for every surviving slug, one key per ingredient index. Soup now has two ingredients, so the valid keys are `soup:0` and `soup:1`. The checked and quantities filters keep only entries whose key is in that set, so both `soup:2` entries disappear, and everything else is kept. The worked change calls this a schema migration that needs no migration code.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Keys checked by slug prefix": `validKeys` contains full `slug:index` keys, not prefixes.
- "The whole document is rejected": filtering is per entry; one bad key never rejects the rest.
- "Only the checked entry is dropped": the quantities filter uses the same `validKeys`.

excerpts.quote: const validKeys = new Set(recipeSlugs.flatMap((slug) => recipes.find((recipe) => recipe.slug === slug)!.ingredients.map((_, i) => `${slug}:${i}`)));
because `validKeys` (line 15) is rebuilt from *today's* ingredient array, not from the stored keys. This is a schema migration that needs no migration code

items.title: Which check drops a number stored as a quantity
items.body:
The key is right: the `typeof`-string check drops it, and a surviving number would reach code typed for strings. The entry `'soup:0': 0` has a **valid key**, so a naive "drop keys I don't recognise" rule keeps it. What removes it is `typeof v === 'string'` on line 23. If it got through, `ingredientsWithQuantities` would put the number `0` where TypeScript believes there is always a string, and the screen and clipboard formatter would use it: a runtime type error the compiler cannot see, arriving from storage.

Why the others are wrong:
- "The length bound": `v.length <= 100` runs after the type check; the type check already rejected it.
- "The key check": the key `soup:0` is valid.
- "Nothing; 0 becomes '0' when saved": `JSON.stringify` keeps numbers as numbers.

excerpts.quote: validKeys.has(key) && typeof v === 'string' && v.length <= 100
The key is valid, so the naive implementation ("drop keys I do not recognise") keeps it; the type check at line 23 is what drops it.

items.title: What survives the recipeSlugs filter
items.body:
The key is right: `['soup']`. The worked change takes this exact input apart in four steps:

1. **Is-array guard**: `recipeSlugs` is an array, so processing continues.
2. **Type check**: `typeof slug === 'string'` drops `42` and `null`, leaving `['soup','soup','missing']`.
3. **Membership check**: `recipes.some(recipe => recipe.slug === slug)` drops `'missing'`, which is a string but not a recipe this cookbook has, leaving `['soup','soup']`.
4. **Dedupe**: `[...new Set(...)]` keeps the first of each, leaving `['soup']`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "[]: mixed types trigger the guard": the guard only checks that the value is an array; bad items are filtered one by one.
- "['soup', 'missing']": membership is checked inside this same filter, not later.
- "['soup', 'soup']": the Set dedupes every surviving slug.

excerpts.quote: ? [...new Set(input.recipeSlugs.filter((slug): slug is string => typeof slug === 'string' && recipes.some((recipe) => recipe.slug === slug)))] : [];
`Set` preserves insertion order, so the first occurrence wins and the list stays stable across reloads. Input: `['soup','soup']`. Output: `['soup']`.
